entry: Creamy [[Dairy|dairy]]-based beverage, traditionally made with [[Milk|milk]] or cream, sugar and whipped eggs, and sometimes with spirits such as [[Brandy|brandy]], [[Rum|rum]] or bourbon. It is traditionally consumed at [[Christmas]] in [[Canada]] and the [[United States]], often from Thanksgiving through the end of the Christmas season. Commercially prepared eggnog is sold in grocery stores during this period. Eggnog flavoring also appears in coffee, tea and desserts such as ice cream. The first printed use of the term appeared in 1788.

*Solanum melongena*, a plant species of the nightshade family Solanaceae, grown worldwide for its edible fruit, typically used as a vegetable in cooking. The plant is also called aubergine and brinjal. The spongy, absorbent fruit is most commonly purple and is botanically a berry. Eggplant is low in macronutrients and micronutrients, but its ability to absorb oils and flavors makes it important in the [[Culinary arts|culinary arts]]. As a member of the genus *Solanum*, the plant is related to the [[Chili pepper|chili pepper]] and [[Potato|potato]], which are of the [[Americas]] region, whereas eggplant is of the [[Eurasia]] region. It was domesticated from the wild nightshade *S. incanum*, probably in two independent domestications in South Asia and East Asia. In 2023 world production was 61 million tonnes, with China and India accounting for 85% of the total. The name eggplant, first recorded in 1763, was originally applied to white cultivars resembling hen's eggs.

Eggs of birds and other animals eaten by humans, chiefly those of [[Chicken|chickens]]. Humans have eaten eggs for millions of years, and people in Southeast Asia began harvesting chicken eggs around 1500 BC. Eggs of ducks and ostriches are eaten much less commonly, as are those of reptiles, amphibians and [[Fish|fish]]; fish eggs are known as roe or caviar. Chickens were most likely domesticated for their eggs before 7500 BC, and [[Selective breeding|selective breeding]] has since produced hens capable of laying more than 300 eggs a year. In the [[Middle Ages]], eggs were forbidden during Lent, although the restriction also let farmers rest their flocks and limit feed use. In 2009 an estimated 62.1 million metric tons of eggs were produced worldwide from approximately 6.4 billion hens.

Most widely spoken vernacular [[Arabic]] variety in [[Egypt]], also called Colloquial Egyptian or Masri. It is part of the Afro-Asiatic language family and originated in the [[Nile|Nile Delta]]. An estimated 111 million Egyptians speak a continuum of [[Dialect|dialects]], and the variety is widely understood across the Arab world because of Egyptian films and other media since the early 20th century. Its written form is used in novels, plays, poems, comics and advertising, while standardized literary Arabic, based on [[Classical Arabic]], is used in most other written media. Its phonetics, grammar and vocabulary were influenced by Coptic, and its vocabulary also by Turkish and by European languages such as French, Italian, Greek and English. Cairene Arabic is by far the most prevalent dialect in the country.

National history museum in [[Cairo]], [[Egypt]], formally the Museum of Egyptian Antiquities. It houses the largest collection of Egyptian antiquities in the world, including over 170,000 items and the funerary equipment of [[Tutankhamun]]. It is one of the largest museums in Africa and was the first national museum established in the [[Middle East]]. The Egyptian government established a museum in 1835 near the Ezbekieh Garden. In 1858 a new museum opened at Boulaq under Auguste Mariette, and in 1889 the collection moved to a palace in [[Giza]]. It was moved again in 1902 to its present site on Tahrir Square. During the 2011 Egyptian revolution, looters damaged mummies and statues and stole around 1,000 objects, nearly all of which were recovered within months.

Formal writing system of [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]] for writing the [[Egyptian language|Egyptian language]], combining ideographic, logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements. In the Middle Kingdom the system used about 900 distinct signs, and cursive forms were used for religious literature on [[Papyrus|papyrus]] and wood. Hieroglyphs are the ultimate ancestor of the [[Phoenician alphabet]], the first widely used phonetic writing system. They are thought to be one of four writing systems developed without outside influence, along with [[Cuneiform|cuneiform]], [[Chinese characters]] and Mayan script. The first decipherable sentence dates to the 28th century BC. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use extend into the 4th century AD, but after pagan temples closed in the 5th century, fluent readers were lost. Jean-François Champollion deciphered the script in the 1820s with the help of the [[Rosetta Stone]].

Extinct branch of the [[Afroasiatic languages|Afro-Asiatic]] language family, spoken in [[Egypt]]. It is one of the earliest known written languages, first recorded in hieroglyphic script in the late 4th millennium BC, and the longest-attested human language, with a written record spanning over 5,000 years. Its classical form, Middle Egyptian, was the vernacular of the Middle Kingdom and remained Egypt's literary language until Christianization in the Roman period. By classical antiquity the spoken language had evolved into Demotic, and later Coptic dialects were written in the [[Greek alphabet]]. These were supplanted by [[Arabic]] after the Arab conquest of Egypt, although Bohairic Coptic remains the liturgical language of the [[Coptic Orthodox Church|Coptic Orthodox]] and Coptic Catholic churches. Linguists have variously linked it with Berber and [[Semitic languages|Semitic]] languages, particularly Arabic and Hebrew.

Collection of myths from [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]] that describe the actions of the gods as a means of understanding the world. Myths appear in writings and art, particularly in [[Hymn|hymns]], ritual texts, funerary texts and temple decoration, though sources rarely contain a complete account of a myth. Egyptians saw time as a series of recurring patterns set by myth, and present events renewed *maat*, the fundamental order of the universe. Major episodes include the creation myths, in which the gods form the universe from primordial chaos; the reign of the sun god [[Ra]] on earth; and the Osiris myth, concerning the struggles of [[Osiris]], [[Isis]] and [[Horus]] against the disruptive god [[Set (deity)|Set]]. The details differ between texts and often seem contradictory, as the myths are primarily metaphorical. Mythology provided the ideological basis for kingship and inspired many religious rituals, and its scenes appeared in tombs, temples and amulets.

Group of 13 genetic connective tissue disorders, named after the dermatologists Edvard Ehlers and Henri-Alexandre Danlos. Symptoms often include loose joints, joint pain, stretchy, velvety skin and abnormal scar formation. Complications may include aortic dissection and [[Scoliosis|scoliosis]]. The condition results from mutations in one or more of 19 genes. No cure is known, and treatment is supportive. Some forms have a normal life expectancy, but those affecting blood vessels generally reduce it. It affects at least one in 5,000 people.

Islamic and [[Druze]] festival, the second of the two main festivals in Islam, also called the Greater or Large Eid. It falls on the 10th of Dhu'l-Hijja, the twelfth and final month of the [[Islamic calendar]], and celebrations are generally carried on for three following days, known as the Tashreeq days. After the Eid prayer in the morning, the ritual sacrifice of a livestock animal, the *udhiyah*, is performed. In Islamic tradition, the festival honors Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son as an act of obedience to God; depending on the narrative, either Ishmael or [[Isaac]] is given the honorific "Sacrifice of God". Pilgrims performing the [[Hajj]] typically perform the tawaf and sa'i on this day, along with the ritual stoning of the Devil on the Eid day and the following days.

Islamic festival held on the first day of *Shawwal*, the tenth month of the [[Islamic calendar]], marking the end of the month-long dawn-to-dusk fast of [[Ramadan]]. It is the first of the two main festivals in Islam, the other being [[Eid al-Adha]]. It begins with a communal [[Prayer|prayer]], followed by visits to relatives, gifts and shared meals, and with food as a central theme the holiday is nicknamed "Sweet Eid" or "Sugar Feast". According to Muslim tradition, [[Muhammad]] instituted the celebration in [[Medina]] after his migration from Mecca. Fasting is forbidden on the day, and obligatory charity, the *zakat al-Fitr*, is paid to the poor before the Eid prayer. The holiday lasts one to three days, depending on the country, and its date shifts about 10–11 days earlier each year in the [[Gregorian calendar]].

[[Wrought iron|Wrought-iron]] lattice tower on the Champ de Mars in Paris, France. The design is attributed to Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier, engineers at the company of [[Gustave Eiffel]], which built the tower from 1887 to 1889 as the centerpiece of the [[World's fair|1889 World's Fair]], also marking the centennial of the [[French Revolution]]. Initially criticized by leading artists and intellectuals, it became a global cultural icon of France. At 330 m (1,083 ft) it is the tallest structure in Paris, and it held the title of the world's tallest man-made structure for 41 years, until the Chrysler Building in New York City was finished in 1930. It received 5,889,000 visitors in 2022. It was designated a monument historique in 1964 and named part of a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 1991.

Concepts from [[Linear algebra|linear algebra]] describing the directions a linear transformation leaves unchanged. An eigenvector is a nonzero vector whose direction is unchanged or reversed by a linear transformation T, so that T(v) = λv for a scalar λ, called the eigenvalue. Eigenvalues may be negative, zero or complex. The prefix *eigen-* comes from the German word for "own" or "characteristic". Because eigenvalues and eigenvectors characterize a transformation, they are used in fields from [[Geology|geology]] to [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]], including stability and vibration analysis, [[Atomic orbital|atomic orbitals]] and facial recognition. In a system with feedback, the largest eigenvalue governs long-term behavior, and its eigenvector is the steady state.

Armed conflict in the Habsburg [[Netherlands|Netherlands]] (c. 1566/1568–1648) between rebel groups and the Spanish government, also called the Dutch Revolt. Its causes included the [[Reformation]], centralization, excessive taxation and the rights and privileges of the Dutch nobility and cities. After [[Philip II of Spain|Philip II]] regained most rebel-held territory, mutinies in the Spanish army caused a general uprising, led by the exiled [[William the Silent]]. The Union of Utrecht proclaimed independence in the 1581 Act of Abjuration and established the Calvinist-dominated Dutch Republic in 1588. France and England recognized the Republic in 1596, and a Twelve Years' Truce was agreed in 1609. When the truce expired in 1621, fighting resumed as part of the [[Thirty Years' War]]. The war ended in 1648 with the Peace of Münster, part of the [[Peace of Westphalia]], under which Spain retained the Southern Netherlands and recognized the Dutch Republic as an independent country.

Equations of [[General relativity|general relativity]] relating the geometry of [[Spacetime|spacetime]] to the distribution of matter and energy within it. [[Albert Einstein|Einstein]] published them in 1915 as a [[Tensor|tensor]] equation relating local spacetime curvature to local energy, momentum and stress. They reduce to Newton's law of gravitation in a weak gravitational field at velocities far below the speed of light. Exact solutions require simplifying assumptions such as symmetry, and they model phenomena such as rotating [[Black hole|black holes]] and the expanding universe. Linearized versions are used to study [[Gravitational wave|gravitational waves]].

Synthetic [[Actinide|actinide]] element with symbol Es and atomic number 99, the seventh transuranium element. It was first identified in December 1952 in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb explosion, and it is named after [[Albert Einstein]]. Its most common isotope, einsteinium-253, has a [[Half-life|half-life]] of 20.47 days and is produced in reactors with a total yield on the order of one milligram per year. It has no practical applications beyond basic research, although in 1955 it was used to synthesize 17 atoms of the new element mendelevium. It is a soft, silvery, paramagnetic metal and is highly radioactive.

Japanese politician, prime minister of Japan from 1964 to 1972. He was the third longest-serving Japanese prime minister and the longest-serving without interruption. A former [[Civil service|civil servant]] in the Ministry of Railways, he joined the [[Liberal Democratic Party (Japan)|Liberal Democratic Party]] and was the younger brother of Nobusuke Kishi, prime minister from 1957 to 1960. He presided over rapid economic growth and normalized diplomatic relations with [[South Korea]]. He secured the return of Okinawa to Japan in 1972 and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1974, a choice that stirred controversy. In 1967 he introduced the Three Non-Nuclear Principles, and in 1968 he signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. Later revelations indicated that he had made secret agreements with the [[United States]] that permitted violations of the principles, which sparked debate in Japan. He resigned in 1972 and was succeeded by Kakuei Tanaka.

Discharge of [[Semen|semen]] from the penis through the [[Urethra|urethra]], normally containing sperm. It is the final stage of male sexual stimulation and an essential component of natural conception. It involves involuntary contractions of the pelvic floor and is normally linked with [[Orgasm|orgasm]]. Males become able to ejaculate during [[Puberty|puberty]], and it can also occur during sleep as a nocturnal emission. Anejaculation is the inability to ejaculate, and retrograde ejaculation is the backward flow of semen into the [[Bladder|bladder]]. A vasectomy alters the composition of the ejaculate as a form of permanent [[Birth control|birth control]].

Mexican former drug lord and top leader of the [[Sinaloa Cartel]], born Joaquín Archivaldo Guzmán Loera. He is believed to be responsible for the deaths of over 34,000 people. He founded his own cartel in 1988, after the arrest of [[Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo]], and oversaw the mass production and smuggling of [[Cocaine|cocaine]], [[Methamphetamine|methamphetamine]] and [[Heroin|heroin]] into the United States. [[Forbes]] ranked him among the most powerful people in the world from 2009 to 2013. He escaped from prison twice, in 2001 and 2015, and in 2019 he was sentenced to [[Life imprisonment|life imprisonment]] in the United States.

Castilian knight and ruler in medieval Spain, prince of Valencia from 1094 to 1099. Born Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, he fought in the armies of both Christian and Muslim rulers and earned the Arabic honorific *as-Sayyid*, meaning "the Lord," which evolved into El Cid. Exiled in 1081, he served the Muslim rulers of [[Zaragoza]], then took [[Valencia]] in 1094 and ruled it as a pluralistic principality with the support of Christians and Muslims alike. After his death his widow, Jimena, inherited the city and held it until 1102, when it was reconquered by the [[Moors]]. He became Spain's most celebrated national hero and the subject of the epic poem *El Cantar de mio Cid*.

Mythical city of gold supposedly located somewhere in South America. The legend originated in 16th-century Spanish accounts of a ruler called El Dorado, or the Golden One, who covered himself in gold dust before washing it off in a sacred lake. It is associated with the Muisca people of present-day [[Colombia]], and later accounts linked it to the installation of a new *zipa*, who made offerings of gold at Lake Guatavita. Spanish expeditions under Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada conquered Muisca territory in 1537. Later expeditions, including those of Gonzalo Pizarro, Francisco Orellana and Walter Raleigh, moved the supposed location to the Amazon and the Guianas. The legend then became associated with Lake Parime, a supposed inland lake that appeared on 17th-century maps before its existence was rejected. Although belief in El Dorado as a real place declined, it became a symbol of fabulous wealth, appearing in *Candide* by [[Voltaire]].

Greek painter, sculptor and architect of the Spanish Renaissance. The name El Greco means "The Greek" in Spanish. He was born in Candia, on [[Crete]], then part of the [[Republic of Venice]] and a center of Post-Byzantine art, and he trained as an icon painter. His work absorbed [[Mannerism]] and the Venetian Renaissance, notably [[Titian]] and Tintoretto. He moved to Rome in 1570 and to [[Toledo, Spain|Toledo]] in 1577, where he worked until his death and painted *View of Toledo* and *Opening of the Fifth Seal*. His dramatic, elongated figures puzzled his contemporaries but were admired in the 20th century, when he was seen as a precursor of [[Expressionism]] and [[Cubism]]. Later artists influenced by him include Francisco Goya, Diego Velázquez and [[Pablo Picasso]].

Global climate phenomenon of fluctuating sea surface temperatures over the tropical [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific Ocean]]. Its warming phase is called El Niño and its cooling phase La Niña, and the Southern Oscillation is the accompanying shift in [[Atmospheric pressure|surface air pressure]]. The phases recur irregularly about every two to seven years and are not easily predictable. El Niño causes short-term spikes in global average surface temperature, lasting about one year, while La Niña causes short-term cooling. The phenomenon disrupts weather across the [[Tropics|tropics]] and beyond, bringing intense storms to some places and droughts to others. The countries most affected are developing countries bordering the Pacific that depend on agriculture and fishing. The term was first recorded in a climate context in 1892, when Captain Camilo Carrillo reported to a geographical congress in [[Lima]] that Peruvian sailors had named the warm current after the Christ Child, as it typically appeared around [[Christmas]].

City (pop., 2020: 678,815) in [[Texas|West Texas]], United States, and county seat of El Paso County. It stands on the [[Rio Grande]] across the border from [[Ciudad Juárez]], Mexico, and forms part of a binational region known as the Borderplex. Some 81% of its residents are Hispanic, making it the second-largest absolute-majority-Hispanic city in the United States, after [[San Antonio]]. The University of Texas at El Paso is the city's primary university, and Fort Bliss, an Army installation, is in the area.

Sovereign country in [[Central America]] on the Pacific coast, bounded by [[Guatemala]] to the northwest and [[Honduras]] to the northeast, with its capital at [[San Salvador]]. Its population was estimated at approximately 6 million in 2024. Spain conquered the region in 1524 and incorporated it into the Viceroyalty of [[New Spain]]. After independence in 1821 and a brief federation with its Central American neighbors, El Salvador became a sovereign republic in 1841. The Salvadoran Civil War (1979–1992) was fought between the government and the Farabundo Martí National Liberation Front, and ended with the Chapultepec Peace Accords. Nearly one million citizens migrated to the [[United States]] between 1980 and 2008. [[Coffee]] once generated roughly 90% of national export revenues. In 2001, El Salvador replaced its national currency, the colón, with the [[United States dollar]].
